catherine-of-braganza.name: Catherine of Braganza
catherine-of-braganza.summary: Queen of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1662 to 1685 through marriage to Charles II, later serving as regent in her native Portugal.

louis-xiv.name: Louis XIV
louis-xiv.summary: King of France from 1643 to 1715, the longest-reigning monarch in history, who built an absolute monarchy centered on the Palace of Versailles.

richard-pynson.name: Richard Pynson
richard-pynson.summary: One of the first printers of English books (c. 1449 – c. 1529), born in Normandy and later a leading London printer, known for high craftsmanship and works like the first English cookery book.

the-boke-of-cokery.name: The Boke of Cokery
the-boke-of-cokery.summary: Believed to be the first cookery book printed in English, produced by Richard Pynson in 1500 and compiled from earlier medieval texts.

the-good-huswifes-jewell.name: The Good Huswifes Jewell
the-good-huswifes-jewell.summary: 1585 English cookery book by Thomas Dawson including recipes for both food and medicines; notable as the first English cookery book with a recipe for sweet potatoes.

hannah-glasse.name: Hannah Glasse
hannah-glasse.summary: An English cookery writer (1708–1770) whose 1747 book The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy became the century's best-selling recipe book, including an early English curry recipe.

the-art-of-cookery-made-plain-and-easy.name: The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy
the-art-of-cookery-made-plain-and-easy.summary: An enormously popular 1747 cookbook by Hannah Glasse that dominated the English-speaking market for a century and included one of the first English recipes for an Indian-style curry.
the-art-of-cookery-made-plain-and-easy.source_title: The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy

clarissa-dickson-wright.name: Clarissa Dickson Wright
clarissa-dickson-wright.summary: English celebrity cook, television personality and writer (1947–2014), best known as one of the Two Fat Ladies on the 1996–1999 cooking programme.

gda-sk.name: Gdańsk
gda-sk.summary: A Baltic port city in northern Poland, historically known as Danzig, a major Hanseatic trading city and later the birthplace of the Solidarity movement in the 1980s.

k-nigsberg.name: Königsberg
k-nigsberg.summary: German city founded in 1255 by the Teutonic Knights, later capital of the Duchy of Prussia and a coronation city of the Prussian monarchy; renamed Kaliningrad after becoming Soviet territory in 1946.

greenock.name: Greenock
greenock.summary: A town in Inverclyde, Scotland, on the south bank of the River Clyde where it widens into the Firth of Clyde, with a 2022 population of about 42,870.

vincent-la-chapelle.name: Vincent La Chapelle
vincent-la-chapelle.summary: French master cook (1690 or 1703 – 1745) who worked for the 4th Earl of Chesterfield and William IV, Prince of Orange.

anne-of-austria.name: Anne of Austria
anne-of-austria.summary: Queen of France from 1615 to 1643 as wife of Louis XIII, and regent for her young son Louis XIV from 1643 to 1651.

maria-theresa-of-spain.name: Maria Theresa of Spain
maria-theresa-of-spain.summary: Queen of France from 1660 to 1683 as wife of Louis XIV; their marriage ended a long France–Spain war, though she held little political influence at the French court.

pont-neuf.name: Pont Neuf
pont-neuf.summary: The oldest standing bridge over the Seine in Paris, built at the tip of the Île de la Cité and named 'New Bridge' to distinguish it from older, house-lined bridges it outlasted.

palais-royal.name: Palais-Royal
palais-royal.summary: A former French royal palace in Paris near the Louvre, built for Cardinal Richelieu in the 1630s and later home to several Dukes of Orléans.

place-des-vosges.name: Place des Vosges
place-des-vosges.summary: The oldest planned square in Paris, originally called the Place Royale, built in the Marais district and a fashionable address for Parisian nobility in the 17th and 18th centuries.

jardin-du-luxembourg.name: Luxembourg Garden
jardin-du-luxembourg.summary: A 23-hectare Paris garden begun in 1612 by Marie de' Medici alongside her new Luxembourg Palace residence, now owned and maintained by the French Senate.

acad-mie-royale-de-peinture-et-de-sculpt.name: Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture
acad-mie-royale-de-peinture-et-de-sculpt.summary: France's premier art institution, founded in Paris in 1648, controlling art teaching and royal commissions until abolished in 1793.
acad-mie-royale-de-peinture-et-de-sculpt.source_title: Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture

portrait-miniature.name: Portrait miniature
portrait-miniature.summary: A small Renaissance-era portrait painting, popular from the 16th century mainly in England and France, often given as an intimate gift before photography replaced the format.

chatsworth-house.name: Chatsworth House
chatsworth-house.summary: A stately home in Derbyshire, England, seat of the Duke of Devonshire, begun by Bess of Hardwick in 1553 and owned by the Cavendish family since 1549.

castle-howard.name: Castle Howard
castle-howard.summary: An English country house in North Yorkshire, home to the Carlisle branch of the Howard family for over 300 years and a well-known filming location.

rococo.name: Rococo
rococo.summary: Ornamental Western style of art, architecture and decoration that emerged in France in the 1730s, marked by fluid curves, asymmetry and pastel colours, later replaced by Neoclassicism.

neoclassicism.name: Neoclassicism
neoclassicism.summary: A Western cultural movement in art, architecture and literature inspired by classical antiquity, born in Rome and reaching its peak in the early-to-mid 19th century.

english-reformation.name: English Reformation
english-reformation.summary: 16th-century break of the Church of England from papal authority, begun after Henry VIII's annulment request was refused, part of the wider European Reformation.

hans-holbein-the-younger.name: Hans Holbein the Younger
hans-holbein-the-younger.summary: German painter and printmaker (c. 1497–1543), regarded as one of the greatest portraitists of the 16th century, known for portraits of Erasmus and work within Thomas More's circle in England.

anthony-van-dyck.name: Anthony van Dyck
anthony-van-dyck.summary: Flemish Baroque painter (1599–1641) who became England's leading court portraitist, especially known for his portraits of Charles I and the aristocracy.

peter-paul-rubens.name: Peter Paul Rubens
peter-paul-rubens.summary: Flemish Baroque painter and diplomat (1577–1640), considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque, known for dramatic, sensuous religious and mythological works.

peter-lely.name: Peter Lely
peter-lely.summary: Dutch-born painter who became England's dominant court portrait painter and was knighted by Charles II in 1680.

godfrey-kneller.name: Godfrey Kneller
godfrey-kneller.summary: German-born British painter (1646-1723) who served as court portraitist to English and British monarchs including Charles II and George I, and painted figures such as Isaac Newton.

christopher-wren.name: Christopher Wren
christopher-wren.summary: English architect, astronomer, mathematician and physicist (1632–1723) who rebuilt 52 London churches after the Great Fire, including St Paul's Cathedral, and led the Royal Society.

john-vanbrugh.name: John Vanbrugh
john-vanbrugh.summary: English architect and playwright (1664–1726), designer of Blenheim Palace and pioneer of English Baroque architecture, also known for Restoration comedies.

nicholas-hawksmoor.name: Nicholas Hawksmoor
nicholas-hawksmoor.summary: English Baroque architect (c. 1661–1736) who worked alongside Christopher Wren and John Vanbrugh on buildings including St Paul's Cathedral, Blenheim Palace and Castle Howard.

blenheim-palace.name: Blenheim Palace
blenheim-palace.summary: A country house in Oxfordshire, England, built 1705–1722 as a reward for the 1st Duke of Marlborough's victory at the Battle of Blenheim, and the birthplace of Winston Churchill.

seaton-delaval-hall.name: Seaton Delaval Hall
seaton-delaval-hall.summary: A Grade I listed English Baroque country house in Northumberland, designed by Sir John Vanbrugh in 1718, later gutted by fire in 1822 and now owned by the National Trust.

guillaume-coustou-the-elder.name: Guillaume Coustou the Elder
guillaume-coustou-the-elder.summary: A French Baroque sculptor (1677–1746) and royal sculptor to Louis XIV and XV, best known for the monumental Marly Horses now in Paris's Place de la Concorde.

marly-horses.name: Marly Horses
marly-horses.summary: Pair of 1743–1745 marble sculptures by Guillaume Coustou showing rearing horses with grooms, commissioned by Louis XV and, after copies replaced them on site, now displayed in the Louvre.

robert-le-lorrain.name: Robert Le Lorrain
robert-le-lorrain.summary: French baroque sculptor (1666-1743), a student of Pierre Puget and François Girardon, best known for The Horses of the Sun relief at the Hôtel de Rohan in Paris.

jean-baptiste-pigalle.name: Jean-Baptiste Pigalle
jean-baptiste-pigalle.summary: A French sculptor (1714–1785) whose work blended baroque and neo-classical styles.

maurice-de-saxe.name: Maurice de Saxe
maurice-de-saxe.summary: Illegitimate son of Augustus II the Strong, he rose to Marshal General of France and became famed for his victories in the 1740–1748 War of the Austrian Succession, notably at Fontenoy.

voltaire.name: Voltaire
voltaire.summary: Pen name of French Enlightenment writer and philosopher François-Marie Arouet (1694-1778), a prolific author known for criticizing the Church and advocating freedom of speech and religion.

nicholas-hilliard.name: Nicholas Hilliard
nicholas-hilliard.summary: English goldsmith and limner (c. 1547–1619) best known for portrait miniatures of the courts of Elizabeth I and James I.

jean-antoine-houdon.name: Jean-Antoine Houdon
jean-antoine-houdon.summary: A French neoclassical sculptor (1741–1828) famous for portrait busts and statues of Enlightenment figures such as Diderot, Rousseau, Voltaire, Franklin and Washington.

mannerism.name: Mannerism
mannerism.summary: A European art style emerging after the Italian High Renaissance around 1520, exaggerating proportion and balance into tension and elegance; it lasted into the late 16th century in Italy.

charles-i-of-england.name: Charles I of England
charles-i-of-england.summary: King of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1625 until his execution in 1649, whose belief in the divine right of kings led to conflict with Parliament.

jacobitism.name: Jacobites
jacobitism.summary: Supporters of a political movement (1688 to the late 1700s) seeking to restore the exiled House of Stuart to the British throne, strongest in Ireland, the Scottish Highlands, and Wales.

james-ii-of-england.name: James II
james-ii-of-england.summary: King of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1685 until deposed in the 1688 Glorious Revolution; the last Catholic monarch of the three kingdoms.

james-francis-edward-stuart.name: James Francis Edward Stuart
james-francis-edward-stuart.summary: The Stuart claimant to the English, Irish and Scottish thrones (1688-1766), known as the Old Pretender, whose backed attempts to reclaim the throne in 1715 and 1719 both failed.

house-of-habsburg.name: Habsburg dynasty
house-of-habsburg.summary: One of Europe's most powerful dynasties, ruling the Holy Roman Empire, Austria and Spain from the Middle Ages until its male line ended in 1740.

diplomatic-revolution-of-1756.name: Diplomatic Revolution of 1756
diplomatic-revolution-of-1756.summary: Reversal of European alliances between 1756's rivals: Austria switched from Britain to France while Prussia allied with Britain, driven chiefly by Austrian statesman Wenzel Anton von Kaunitz.

commonwealth-of-england.name: Commonwealth of England
commonwealth-of-england.summary: The republic that replaced the Kingdom of England from 1649 to 1660, after the execution of Charles I, with power held mainly by Parliament and a Council of State.

charles-ii-of-england.name: Charles II of England
charles-ii-of-england.summary: King of Scotland from 1649 and of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1660 until 1685, restored to the throne after years of exile following the English Civil War.

rump-parliament.name: Rump Parliament
rump-parliament.summary: What remained of England's Long Parliament after Pride's Purge in 1648 removed members opposed to trying King Charles I; dissolved by Oliver Cromwell in 1653.

battle-of-worcester.name: Battle of Worcester
battle-of-worcester.summary: The last major battle of England's Wars of the Three Kingdoms, fought on 3 September 1651, in which Oliver Cromwell's Parliamentarian army decisively defeated Charles II's Royalist force.

oliver-cromwell.name: Oliver Cromwell
oliver-cromwell.summary: English statesman and soldier (1599–1658) who led Parliamentarian forces in the civil wars, backed the execution of Charles I, and ruled as Lord Protector until his death.

the-protectorate.name: The Protectorate
the-protectorate.summary: British republic (1653–1659), formally the Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland, ruled by a Lord Protector, first Oliver Cromwell and then his son Richard.

lord-protector.name: Lord Protector
lord-protector.summary: A British constitutional title for a head of state, sometimes given to a regent acting for an absent monarch.

war-of-devolution.name: War of Devolution
war-of-devolution.summary: An 1667–1668 war in which France under Louis XIV occupied parts of the Spanish Netherlands and Franche-Comté, claiming these territories had 'devolved' to him through his marriage to Maria Theresa of Spain.

franco-dutch-war.name: Franco-Dutch War
franco-dutch-war.summary: Conflict fought mainly between France and the Dutch Republic from 1672 to 1678, in which France nearly overran the Netherlands before the war ended with the 1678 Peace of Nijmegen.

artois.name: Artois
artois.summary: A region of northern France of about 4,000 square kilometres and roughly one million people, whose main cities include Arras, Saint-Omer, Lens and Béthune.

county-of-burgundy.name: County of Burgundy
county-of-burgundy.summary: A feudal territory also called Franche-Comté, ruled by its own counts from 982 to 1678 and later granted autonomy within the Holy Roman Empire, distinct from the neighboring Duchy of Burgundy.

james-butler-1st-duke-of-ormond.name: James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond
james-butler-1st-duke-of-ormond.summary: An Anglo-Irish statesman and soldier (1610-1688) who commanded government forces in Ireland and negotiated a Royalist-Confederate alliance shortly before Charles I's execution.

battle-of-rathmines.name: Battle of Rathmines
battle-of-rathmines.summary: A 2 August 1649 battle near Dublin in which Commonwealth forces under Michael Jones routed a larger Irish Confederate-Royalist army under the Earl of Ormond, securing Dublin and enabling Cromwell's conquest of Ireland.

robert-blake-admiral.name: Robert Blake
robert-blake-admiral.summary: English naval officer (1598-1657) who served under Oliver Cromwell and is regarded as the chief founder of England's naval supremacy, though his achievements were later downplayed after the Stuart Restoration.

prince-rupert-of-the-rhine.name: Prince Rupert of the Rhine
prince-rupert-of-the-rhine.summary: An English-German army officer and admiral, grandson of James VI and I, who became the senior Royalist cavalry commander during the English Civil War.

new-model-army.name: New Model Army
new-model-army.summary: A professional standing army raised by England's Parliamentarians in 1645 during the Civil War, which helped defeat the Royalists and later conquered Scotland and Ireland under Oliver Cromwell.

covenanters.name: Covenanters
covenanters.summary: A 17th-century Scottish movement supporting a Presbyterian Church of Scotland, whose 1638 National Covenant led to war with the king and later a shifting alliance with English Parliamentarians and Royalists.

confederate-ireland.name: Irish Confederates
confederate-ireland.summary: Catholic aristocrats, gentry, clergy and military leaders who formed a self-governing confederation controlling up to two-thirds of Ireland from 1642 to 1652, seeking an end to anti-Catholic discrimination.

irish-rebellion-of-1641.name: Irish Rebellion of 1641
irish-rebellion-of-1641.summary: An uprising begun on 23 October 1641 by Irish gentry and officers seeking to end English domination of Ireland and recover confiscated lands, which grew into the Irish Confederate Wars.

battle-of-culloden.name: Battle of Culloden
battle-of-culloden.summary: The 1746 battle near Inverness where British government forces crushed the Jacobite army of Charles Edward Stuart, ending his bid to restore the Stuarts and Jacobitism as a political force.

house-of-hanover.name: House of Hanover
house-of-hanover.summary: A German royal house that ruled Hanover and, from 1714, Great Britain and Ireland, ending with Queen Victoria's death in 1901.

george-i-of-great-britain.name: George I
george-i-of-great-britain.summary: First British monarch of the House of Hanover, reigning from 1714 until 1727, during a period when real power increasingly shifted to a prime minister-led cabinet.

basil-williams-historian.name: Basil Williams
basil-williams-historian.summary: An English historian who lived from 1867 to 1950.

eighty-years-war.name: Eighty Years' War
eighty-years-war.summary: Also called the Dutch Revolt, an armed conflict from around 1566 to 1648 between Dutch rebels and the Spanish government, ending in recognition of the Dutch Republic.

ivan-sirko.name: Ivan Sirko
ivan-sirko.summary: A Zaporozhian Cossack military leader and Koshovyi Otaman (c. 1605–1680), undefeated in battle and famed across Europe for his campaigns against the Ottoman Empire and Crimean Khanate.

alexander-pope.name: Alexander Pope
alexander-pope.summary: An English poet, translator and satirist (1688–1744) of the Enlightenment, best known for The Rape of the Lock, The Dunciad and his translations of Homer.

the-rape-of-the-lock.name: The Rape of the Lock
the-rape-of-the-lock.summary: Mock-heroic narrative poem by Alexander Pope, first published in 1712 and expanded by 1717, among the most cited examples of high burlesque in English poetry.

the-dunciad.name: The Dunciad
the-dunciad.summary: Mock-heroic narrative poem by Alexander Pope (1728–1743) celebrating the goddess Dulness and her agents bringing decay and tastelessness to Great Britain.

charles-perrault.name: Charles Perrault
charles-perrault.summary: French author (1628–1703) who founded the fairy tale genre with his 1697 collection including 'Little Red Riding Hood,' 'Cinderella' and 'Sleeping Beauty,' later influencing the Brothers Grimm.

henriette-julie-de-murat.name: Henriette-Julie de Murat
henriette-julie-de-murat.summary: French aristocratic writer (1668 to 1716) linked to the Baroque Précieuses movement and one of the creators of the literary fairy tale genre.

madame-d-aulnoy.name: Madame d'Aulnoy
madame-d-aulnoy.summary: French author (1652-1705) known for literary fairy tales; her 1697 collection coined the genre's name and introduced the first "Prince Charming."

william-tyndale.name: William Tyndale
william-tyndale.summary: English Biblical scholar (c. 1494–1536) whose English Bible translation, the first from Hebrew and Greek and to use the printing press, became a landmark of the Protestant Reformation before his execution.

geneva-bible.name: Geneva Bible
geneva-bible.summary: An English Protestant Bible translation from 1560, the first English Bible translated entirely from the original languages, used by Shakespeare and carried to America on the Mayflower.

king-james-version.name: King James Version
king-james-version.summary: An English translation of the Bible commissioned in 1604 and published in 1611, noted for its literary style and its lasting influence on English language and literature.

antoine-galland.name: Antoine Galland
antoine-galland.summary: French orientalist and archaeologist (1646–1715), the first European translator of One Thousand and One Nights, whose version appeared in twelve volumes from 1704 to 1717.

denis-diderot.name: Denis Diderot
denis-diderot.summary: A French Enlightenment philosopher and writer (1713-1784) best known as co-founder and chief editor of the Encyclopédie, which was banned by the Church and French government for its secular tone.

oliver-goldsmith.name: Oliver Goldsmith
oliver-goldsmith.summary: Anglo-Irish writer (1728–1774) known for the novel The Vicar of Wakefield, the play She Stoops to Conquer, and the poem The Deserted Village.

richard-brinsley-sheridan.name: Richard Brinsley Sheridan
richard-brinsley-sheridan.summary: Anglo-Irish playwright and Whig politician (1751–1816) who wrote The Rivals and The School for Scandal and owned London's Theatre Royal, Drury Lane.

the-vicar-of-wakefield.name: The Vicar of Wakefield
the-vicar-of-wakefield.summary: An 1766 sentimental novel by Anglo-Irish writer Oliver Goldsmith (1728–1774), one of the most widely read 18th-century English novels, following the Primrose family's fall from prosperity and eventual return to good standing.

she-stoops-to-conquer.name: She Stoops to Conquer
she-stoops-to-conquer.summary: An 18th-century comedy by Oliver Goldsmith, first performed in London in 1773, remaining a popular comedy of manners built on mistaken identities and class satire.

restoration-comedy.name: Restoration comedy
restoration-comedy.summary: English theatrical comedy of 1660-1710, known for sexually explicit humor and topical plots, that flourished after theatres reopened under Charles II and featured the first professional actresses.

th-ophile-de-viau.name: Théophile de Viau
th-ophile-de-viau.summary: French Baroque poet and dramatist who lived from 1590 to 1626.

charles-de-saint-vremond.name: Charles de Saint-Évremond
charles-de-saint-vremond.summary: French soldier, essayist and literary critic (1613–1703) who lived in exile in England after 1661 and is one of the few foreigners buried in Poets' Corner, Westminster Abbey.

epicurus.name: Epicurus
epicurus.summary: Greek philosopher (341–270 BC) who founded Epicureanism, teaching that managing desires, removing fears, and friendship lead to a pleasant, happy life; he taught at his school 'The Garden' in Athens.

petronius.name: Petronius
petronius.summary: Roman courtier under Emperor Nero (c. 27–66 AD), generally believed to be the author of the satirical novel Satyricon.

william-shakespeare.name: William Shakespeare
william-shakespeare.summary: English playwright, poet and actor (c. 1564–1616), widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language, known for about 39 plays and 154 sonnets.

antony-and-cleopatra.name: Antony and Cleopatra
antony-and-cleopatra.summary: A tragedy by William Shakespeare, first performed around 1607, dramatizing the relationship between Mark Antony and Cleopatra based on Plutarch's Lives.

plutarch.name: Plutarch
plutarch.summary: A Greek and Roman philosopher, historian and biographer (before 50–after 120 AD) best known for Parallel Lives, biographies of famous Greeks and Romans.

cleopatra.name: Cleopatra
cleopatra.summary: Last active Hellenistic pharaoh, ruling Ptolemaic Egypt from 51 to 30 BC; her death marked Egypt becoming a Roman province and the end of the Hellenistic period.

elizabeth-i.name: Elizabeth I
elizabeth-i.summary: Queen of England and Ireland from 1558 to 1603, the last Tudor monarch, whose reign gave its name to the Elizabethan era.

miguel-de-cervantes.name: Miguel de Cervantes
miguel-de-cervantes.summary: A Spanish writer (1547–1616) regarded as the greatest in the Spanish language, best known for Don Quixote, often called the first modern novel.

novelas-ejemplares.name: Novelas ejemplares
novelas-ejemplares.summary: A collection of novellas and stories by Miguel de Cervantes, written between 1590 and 1612 and printed in 1613, mixing idealized and realistic styles.

picaresque-novel.name: Picaresque novel
picaresque-novel.summary: A genre of prose fiction following the episodic adventures of a roguish, low-born hero living by his wits in a corrupt society, beginning with the Spanish novel Lazarillo de Tormes in 1554.

lazarillo-de-tormes.name: Lazarillo de Tormes
lazarillo-de-tormes.summary: An anonymously published Spanish novella from 1554, containing anticlerical content, considered the first work to establish the picaresque satirical novel.

the-rivals.name: The Rivals
the-rivals.summary: Richard Brinsley Sheridan's first play, a five-act comedy of manners first performed in 1775, whose character Mrs Malaprop gave her name to the malapropism.

covent-garden.name: Covent Garden
covent-garden.summary: A district in central London known for its former fruit-and-vegetable market, now shops and street performers, and for the Royal Opera House; Henry VIII granted the land to the Earl of Bedford's family in 1552.

the-school-for-scandal.name: The School for Scandal
the-school-for-scandal.summary: Comedy of manners by Richard Brinsley Sheridan, first performed in London in 1777.

francis-bacon.name: Francis Bacon
francis-bacon.summary: English philosopher and statesman (1561–1626) who served as Attorney General and Lord Chancellor under King James I; called the father of empiricism for arguing science should rest on careful observation and inductive reasoning.

new-atlantis.name: New Atlantis
new-atlantis.summary: A 1626 utopian novel by Francis Bacon depicting an ideal land, Bensalem, and its research institution Salomon's House, which foreshadowed the modern research university.

thomas-more.name: Thomas More
thomas-more.summary: An English lawyer, statesman and Renaissance humanist (1478–1535) who wrote Utopia and was executed for refusing to accept Henry VIII's break with the Catholic Church.

utopia-book.name: Utopia
utopia-book.summary: A 1516 work of fiction and political satire by Thomas More, written in Latin, depicting a fictional island society's customs.

commedia-dell-arte.name: Commedia dell'arte
commedia-dell-arte.summary: An early form of professional theatre from Italy, popular across Europe from the 16th to 18th centuries, known for masked stock characters and improvised comic performances.

moli-re.name: Molière
moli-re.summary: French playwright, actor and poet (1622–1673) regarded as one of the greatest writers in the French language, whose comedies are still widely performed today.

michel-de-montaigne.name: Michel de Montaigne
michel-de-montaigne.summary: French Renaissance writer (1533–1592) who popularised the essay as a literary genre, blending anecdote with intellectual insight and the sceptical motto 'What do I know?'

spenserian-stanza.name: Spenserian stanza
spenserian-stanza.summary: A nine-line verse form invented by Edmund Spenser for his epic poem The Faerie Queene (1590 to 1596), with a fixed rhyme scheme.

edmund-spenser.name: Edmund Spenser
edmund-spenser.summary: An English poet (c.1552-1599) best known for The Faerie Queene, an epic allegory honouring the Tudor dynasty and Elizabeth I.

samuel-daniel.name: Samuel Daniel
samuel-daniel.summary: English poet, playwright and historian (1562–1619) of the late-Elizabethan and Jacobean eras, best known for the sonnet cycle Delia.

isaac-newton.name: Isaac Newton
isaac-newton.summary: English mathematician and physicist (1642–1727) whose 1687 Principia established the laws of motion and universal gravitation, founding classical mechanics.

philosophi-naturalis-principia-mathemati.name: Principia Mathematica
philosophi-naturalis-principia-mathemati.summary: Isaac Newton's 1687 book setting out his laws of motion and law of universal gravitation, forming the mathematical foundation of classical mechanics.

paris-observatory.name: Paris Observatory
paris-observatory.summary: Established in 1667, the world's oldest observatory still in operation, founded to map the skies and aid navigation under Louis XIV.

french-academy-of-sciences.name: French Academy of Sciences
french-academy-of-sciences.summary: A learned society founded in 1666 by Louis XIV to encourage French scientific research, at the forefront of European science in the 17th and 18th centuries.

pierre-gassendi.name: Pierre Gassendi
pierre-gassendi.summary: French philosopher, priest, astronomer and mathematician (1592–1655) who tracked the 1631 transit of Mercury and tried to reconcile Epicurean atomism with Christianity.

rudolphine-tables.name: Rudolphine Tables
rudolphine-tables.summary: A star catalogue and planetary tables published by Johannes Kepler in 1627 using Tycho Brahe's observations, considerably more precise than earlier tables for finding planetary positions.

johannes-kepler.name: Johannes Kepler
johannes-kepler.summary: German astronomer and mathematician (1571–1630) whose laws of planetary motion made him a key figure of the Scientific Revolution; he worked under Tycho Brahe and later as imperial mathematician to Emperor Rudolf II.

richard-popkin.name: Richard Popkin
richard-popkin.summary: American philosopher (1923–2005) who specialized in the history of Enlightenment philosophy and early modern anti-dogmatism, and an acclaimed scholar of Christian millenarianism and Jewish messianism.

edward-la-zouche-11th-baron-zouche.name: Sir Edward Zouche
edward-la-zouche-11th-baron-zouche.summary: English diplomat (1556 to 1625) remembered for his lone vote against condemning Mary, Queen of Scots, and for a stag hunt where his guest, the Archbishop of Canterbury, accidentally killed a man.

winchester.name: Winchester
winchester.summary: Cathedral city in Hampshire, England, that grew from the Roman town of Venta Belgarum and was one of the most important cities in Anglo-Saxon England.

weald.name: The Weald
weald.summary: A once-forested region of South East England between the North and South Downs, its name meaning 'woodland' in Old English.

roundhead.name: Roundheads
roundhead.summary: Supporters of the Parliament of England during the English Civil War (1642–1651), fighting King Charles I's Royalist Cavaliers to give Parliament supreme control of government.

cavalier.name: Cavaliers
cavalier.summary: Originally a term of abuse from Roundheads for wealthy royalist supporters of Charles I and Charles II in the English Civil War, later adopted by the Royalists themselves.

interregnum-england.name: The Interregnum (England)
interregnum-england.summary: The period of republican government in England between the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649 and the return of his son Charles II in 1660.

diggers.name: The Diggers
diggers.summary: 17th-century English religious and political dissidents, led by Gerrard Winstanley and William Everard from 1649, who split from the Levellers and farmed common land to build small, egalitarian rural communities.

gerrard-winstanley.name: Gerrard Winstanley
gerrard-winstanley.summary: English religious reformer and political philosopher (1609–1676) who founded the Diggers, occupying common land to farm it after it had been enclosed and privatised.

treaty-of-the-pyrenees.name: Treaty of the Pyrenees
treaty-of-the-pyrenees.summary: Treaty signed 7 November 1659 by Louis XIV of France and Philip IV of Spain, ending the Franco-Spanish War that had begun in 1635.

roussillon.name: Roussillon
roussillon.summary: A historical province of southern France corresponding to the former County of Roussillon and part of the County of Cerdagne in the old Principality of Catalonia.

catalan-republic-1640-1641.name: Catalan Republic
catalan-republic-1640-1641.summary: A short-lived state proclaimed by Catalonia's assembly in 1641 under French protection during the Reapers' War, before union with France and later reabsorption by Spain.

franco-spanish-war-1635-1659.name: Franco-Spanish War
franco-spanish-war-1635-1659.summary: Conflict between France and Spain from 1635 to 1659, fought mainly in northern Italy, the Spanish Netherlands and the Rhineland, ending with the 1659 Treaty of the Pyrenees.

national-constituent-assembly-france.name: National Constituent Assembly
national-constituent-assembly-france.summary: The French revolutionary body that replaced the National Assembly in July 1789 and governed until 1791, when it was succeeded by the Legislative Assembly.

ren-descartes.name: René Descartes
ren-descartes.summary: A French philosopher, mathematician and scientist (1596–1650) known for "I think, therefore I am" and for founding analytic geometry.

cogito-ergo-sum.name: Cogito, ergo sum
cogito-ergo-sum.summary: Latin for "I think, therefore I am," the foundational principle of René Descartes's philosophy, first published in French in his 1637 Discourse on the Method.

declaration-of-the-rights-of-man-and-of-.name: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
declaration-of-the-rights-of-man-and-of-.summary: A 1789 French Revolutionary document asserting universal human rights, drafted with input from Lafayette and Jefferson, that became a foundation of French constitutional law.
declaration-of-the-rights-of-man-and-of-.source_title: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

montesquieu.name: Montesquieu
montesquieu.summary: French political philosopher (1689 to 1755) known for developing the theory of separation of powers and for his 1748 book The Spirit of Law, which influenced the US Constitution.

persian-letters.name: Persian Letters
persian-letters.summary: A 1721 satirical novel by Montesquieu describing two fictional Persian noblemen's experiences in France under Louis XIV, criticising French society through their outsider eyes.

pierre-charron.name: Pierre Charron
pierre-charron.summary: French Catholic theologian (1541–1603) known for controversial skepticism and for separating ethics from religion as its own philosophical discipline.

antoine-arnauld.name: Antoine Arnauld
antoine-arnauld.summary: French Catholic theologian, philosopher and mathematician (1612–1694), a leading intellectual of the Jansenist Port-Royal group.

pierre-nicole.name: Pierre Nicole
pierre-nicole.summary: French writer (1625–1695), one of the most distinguished of the French Jansenists.

port-royal-logic.name: Port-Royal Logic
port-royal-logic.summary: An influential 1662 textbook on logic by Antoine Arnauld and Pierre Nicole that helped popularize key ideas about definitions and classes.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

ch-teau-de-vincennes.name: Château de Vincennes
ch-teau-de-vincennes.summary: A former fortress and royal residence on the edge of Paris, largely built between 1361 and 1369, known for its tall keep and later used as a prison and military headquarters.

philippe-ii-duke-of-orl-ans.name: Philippe II, Duke of Orléans
philippe-ii-duke-of-orl-ans.summary: French prince who served as Regent of the Kingdom of France from 1715 to 1723 during the minority of the young Louis XV.

jacques-b-nigne-bossuet.name: Bossuet
jacques-b-nigne-bossuet.summary: French Catholic bishop and theologian (1627–1704) who served as Bishop of Meaux from 1681, renowned as a brilliant preacher and stylist of French prose.

edict-of-nantes.name: Edict of Nantes
edict-of-nantes.summary: An edict issued in 1598 by King Henry IV of France granting religious tolerance to Protestant Huguenots while Catholicism remained the state religion; it was revoked by Louis XIV in 1685.

richard-simon-priest.name: Richard Simon
richard-simon-priest.summary: French priest and Oratorian (1638–1712) who was an influential biblical critic, orientalist and controversialist.

isaac-la-peyr-re.name: Isaac La Peyrère
isaac-la-peyr-re.summary: French theologian and writer (1596–1676) best known for his Pre-Adamite hypothesis, which challenged the biblical account of human origins in Genesis.

com-die-fran-aise.name: Comédie-Française
com-die-fran-aise.summary: A state theatre founded in Paris in 1680, the oldest active theatre company in the world, nicknamed 'the House of Molière' after its best-known playwright.

jean-baptiste-colbert.name: Jean-Baptiste Colbert
jean-baptiste-colbert.summary: A French statesman (1619–1683) who served as Louis XIV's First Minister of State from 1661, reshaping France's economy and finances in a policy later called Colbertism.

huguenots.name: Huguenots
huguenots.summary: French Protestants of the Reformed Calvinist tradition, concentrated in southern and western France, who made up about 10% of the population before the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572 and faced later persecution under Louis XIV.

st-bartholomew-s-day-massacre.name: St. Bartholomew's Day massacre
st-bartholomew-s-day-massacre.summary: A wave of Catholic mob violence and targeted killings of Protestant Huguenots in France in 1572, beginning in Paris and spreading nationwide, a turning point in the French Wars of Religion.

french-wars-of-religion.name: French Wars of Religion
french-wars-of-religion.summary: Civil wars between French Catholics and Protestant Huguenots from 1562 to 1598 that killed two to four million people and ended with the Edict of Nantes.

louis-xiii.name: Louis XIII
louis-xiii.summary: King of France from 1610 to 1643, who relied on chief ministers Luynes and Cardinal Richelieu, and co-founded the Académie française.

dragonnades.name: Dragonnades
dragonnades.summary: A policy under Louis XIV from 1681 that billeted soldiers in Huguenot homes to pressure French Protestants into converting to Catholicism.

james-vi-and-i.name: James VI and I
james-vi-and-i.summary: King of Scotland from 1567 and of England and Ireland from 1603 until his death in 1625, uniting the crowns while the kingdoms remained separately governed.

north-berwick-witch-trials.name: North Berwick witch trials
north-berwick-witch-trials.summary: 1590 trials in East Lothian, Scotland of over 70 people accused of witchcraft, among the best known of Scotland's many early modern witch trials.

daemonologie.name: Daemonologie
daemonologie.summary: A 1597 treatise by King James VI and I on witchcraft and demonology, written partly to counter sceptics, framing witchcraft as treason against God and endorsing witch hunts.

cardinal-richelieu.name: Cardinal Richelieu
cardinal-richelieu.summary: A French Catholic cardinal and statesman who served as Louis XIII's chief minister from 1624 to 1642, strengthening royal power and opposing Habsburg influence during the Thirty Years' War.

acad-mie-fran-aise.name: Académie Française
acad-mie-fran-aise.summary: France's principal authority on the French language, established in 1635, made up of forty lifetime members who publish an official dictionary.

michel-de-marolles.name: Michel de Marolles
michel-de-marolles.summary: French churchman and translator, known as the abbé de Marolles, whose collection of 123,000 prints, bought by Louis XIV in 1667, founded the royal print collection.
